title: Applied Anatomy: Procedures & Access
summary: See how precise trunk anatomy guides needles, drains, incisions and nerve blocks safely in clinical practice.

lessons.title: Triangle of Safety: Chest Drains and Thoracentesis

levels.kid:
Your lungs sit inside your chest like two balloons. Around each balloon is a thin, slippery bag. Sometimes air or fluid sneaks into that bag and squashes the balloon, so breathing gets hard.

Doctors can fix this with a thin tube or a needle that lets the air or fluid out. But they must pick the right spot. The chest has bones called ribs, and under each rib hides a little bundle of a vein, an artery and a nerve, like wires tucked under a shelf.

So doctors go in at the top edge of a rib, away from those wires. They also use a safe zone on the side of the chest, under the armpit, called the **triangle of safety**. Ultrasound helps them see inside first.
levels.hs:
The **pleura** is a thin double layer around each lung. Between the layers is the **pleural space**, which normally holds only a thin film of fluid. If air collects there (a **pneumothorax**) or fluid or blood does (a **pleural effusion** or **hemothorax**), the lung cannot fully expand.

Two procedures drain it:
- **Thoracentesis**: a needle or thin catheter removes fluid, often to test it or ease breathlessness.
- **Chest drain (tube thoracostomy)**: a tube stays in to keep draining air, blood or fluid.

The usual site for a chest drain is the **triangle of safety**, on the side of the chest. Its borders are:
- the edge of the **pectoralis major** muscle in front,
- the edge of the **latissimus dorsi** muscle behind,
- a line at the level of the nipple (about the **5th intercostal space**) below,
- with the top point just below the armpit.

This area avoids big muscles, breast tissue and the internal thoracic artery near the sternum. Going lower risks hitting the diaphragm, liver or spleen.

Each rib has a **neurovascular bundle** (vein, artery, nerve) running in a groove under its lower edge. That is why the tube or needle goes **just over the top of the rib below**.

Example: a young man with a large spontaneous pneumothorax gets a drain in the 5th space, mid-axillary line, and his lung re-expands.
levels.college:
**The pleural space.** Visceral pleura covers the lung; parietal pleura lines the chest wall, diaphragm and mediastinum. The potential space between them has negative pressure that keeps the lung expanded. Air or fluid breaks this coupling, and the lung recoils.

**The triangle of safety** (British Thoracic Society) is bounded by:
- anterior: lateral border of pectoralis major
- posterior: lateral border (anterior edge) of latissimus dorsi
- inferior: a horizontal line at the level of the nipple, roughly the 5th intercostal space
- apex: just below the axilla

The usual entry is the **4th or 5th intercostal space, mid-axillary line**. Why here:
- Thin wall: mostly serratus anterior and intercostals, so less muscle to cross.
- Avoids the **internal thoracic vessels**, about 1 cm lateral to the sternum.
- Stays above the diaphragm, which rises toward the 5th rib on expiration and higher if the abdomen pushes up. Placing the drain too low risks liver (right) or spleen (left) injury.
- Avoids the **long thoracic nerve**, which runs on serratus anterior posterior to the mid-axillary line; injury causes winged scapula.

**The intercostal space.** The neurovascular bundle runs in the **costal groove** under each rib in the order **VAN** (vein, artery, nerve, top to bottom), between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles. Instruments pass along the **superior border of the lower rib**. Collateral branches run along the upper border of the rib below, so hugging the upper edge closely, not the mid-space, is the goal.

**Thoracentesis** for effusion is often done posteriorly with the patient sitting and leaning forward, guided by ultrasound, typically a few spaces below the top of the effusion and above the diaphragm, lateral to the paraspinal muscles.

**Second intercostal space, midclavicular line** is the classic needle decompression site for tension pneumothorax, though lateral sites are now often preferred.
levels.phd:
The triangle's logic is about layered structures and how they move. Posteriorly near the spine, intercostal arteries are **tortuous** and lie mid-space, not protected by the costal groove; studies using CT angiography show the artery becomes reliably sheltered under the rib only some distance lateral to the spine, with exposure greatest within roughly 6 cm of the midline and in older patients, whose arteries grow more tortuous. This is why posterior thoracentesis is kept well lateral to the paraspinal muscles.

**Diaphragmatic excursion** is the main hazard in low entries. The domes move several centimetres between expiration and inspiration; the right dome sits higher because of the liver. Ultrasound has largely replaced percussion for marking sites, and BTS guidance (2010, updated 2023) recommends image guidance for pleural fluid procedures, which lowers pneumothorax and organ puncture rates.

**Needle decompression.** ATLS recommendations shifted (10th edition) from the 2nd intercostal space midclavicular line to the **4th/5th space just anterior to the mid-axillary line** in adults, because CT studies showed chest wall thickness at the 2nd space often exceeds the length of a standard cannula, causing failure. The midclavicular site also risks drifting medially toward the internal thoracic artery and great vessels.

**Drain types.** Small-bore Seldinger drains are now standard for most pneumothoraces and free-flowing effusions; large-bore drains via blunt dissection remain favoured in trauma hemothorax. Trocar insertion is discouraged because of lung, heart and great-vessel perforation reports.

**Re-expansion pulmonary edema** after rapid lung re-expansion is thought to involve capillary injury from sudden negative pressure and reperfusion; risk rises with large, long-standing collapse. Whether limiting drainage volume or monitoring pleural pressure (manometry) is the better safeguard is still debated; chest discomfort during drainage is commonly used as a stop signal.
levels.expert:
Practical pitfalls cluster around patient factors that distort the textbook triangle.

- **Body habitus.** In obesity, the lateral wall can be thick and landmarks unreliable; ultrasound measures wall depth and confirms the pleural line. In thin or cachectic patients, the margin above the lung or heart is small.
- **Raised hemidiaphragm.** Phrenic palsy, hepatomegaly, ascites, pregnancy or lobar collapse lift the diaphragm, making a 5th-space entry intra-abdominal. Always confirm effusion depth over a full respiratory cycle.
- **Positioning.** Arm abducted behind the head opens the triangle; supine trauma patients may need a slightly more anterior approach at the mid-axillary line.
- **Loculated effusions and empyema.** Septations defeat blind drainage; image-guided placement into the largest pocket is needed. Intrapleural tPA with DNase (MIST-2 trial) improved drainage in pleural infection versus either agent alone.
- **Malignant effusion.** Indwelling pleural catheters (tunnelled, managed at home) are an alternative to talc pleurodesis; trials such as TIME2 and AMPLE showed similar symptom relief with fewer hospital days.

**Complications to anticipate:** intercostal artery laceration (can cause rapid hemothorax, may need angioembolisation or surgery), subcutaneous emphysema, drain misplacement into the fissure or subcutaneous tissue, and organ injury below the diaphragm. A drain that does not swing with respiration may be kinked, blocked or extrapleural. Clamping a bubbling drain risks converting a pneumothorax to tension physiology.

**Conservative care** is expanding: the PSP trial (Brown et al., NEJM 2020) found conservative management of moderate-to-large primary spontaneous pneumothorax non-inferior to drainage in selected patients, with fewer complications. Ambulatory devices with one-way valves are another option.

Open questions include optimal drain size for hemothorax (small-bore appears comparable in several studies), the true safe zone for intercostal arteries in elderly patients, and whether pleural manometry reliably prevents re-expansion edema.

keyPoints: Air or fluid in the pleural space collapses the lung and may need draining
Triangle of safety: pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi, nipple-level line, apex below axilla
Usual drain site is the 4th/5th intercostal space, mid-axillary line
Neurovascular bundle (VAN) runs under each rib, so go over the top of the rib below
Low entries risk diaphragm, liver or spleen; medial entries risk internal thoracic vessels
Ultrasound guidance makes pleural procedures safer

The midclavicular site injures the long thoracic nerve

advancedTest.q: Why is posterior thoracentesis kept well lateral to the paraspinal muscles?
choices: Intercostal arteries run tortuous and unshielded there
The diaphragm rises highest right beside the vertebral column
The lung is most firmly adherent to the chest wall medially

choices: Entering the abdomen below a raised diaphragm

The lung has certainly fully re-expanded

lessons.title: Pericardiocentesis and the Anatomy of Cardiac Tamponade

levels.kid:
Your heart lives inside a thin, tough bag called the **pericardium**. Between the bag and the heart there is a tiny bit of slippery fluid, like oil on a bike chain, so the heart can beat smoothly.

Sometimes too much fluid or blood fills the bag. The bag is strong and does not stretch quickly. So the extra fluid squeezes the heart, like a fist squeezing a water balloon. The heart cannot fill up with blood, so it cannot pump well. This is called **tamponade**, and it is an emergency.

Doctors can fix it by sliding a thin needle into the bag to drain the fluid. They use an ultrasound picture to guide the needle safely. Then the heart can fill and pump again.
levels.hs:
The heart sits in the **pericardium**, a two-layer sac. The outer **fibrous pericardium** is tough and barely stretchy. Inside, the **serous pericardium** has a layer on the heart surface and a layer lining the sac. Between them is the **pericardial cavity**, which normally holds roughly 15 to 50 mL of lubricating fluid.

A **pericardial effusion** is extra fluid in this space. If it builds up faster than the fibrous sac can stretch, pressure rises and squeezes the heart. This is **cardiac tamponade**. The thin-walled right atrium and right ventricle collapse first, because they fill at low pressure. Less blood enters the heart, so less is pumped out and blood pressure falls.

Speed matters more than volume. A stab wound can cause tamponade with only 100 to 200 mL of blood. A slowly growing effusion from cancer may reach a litre or more before it causes trouble.

**Beck's triad** is the classic sign set:
- Low blood pressure
- Swollen neck veins (raised jugular venous pressure)
- Muffled heart sounds

The treatment is **pericardiocentesis**, draining the fluid with a needle. Today it is usually guided by echocardiography (heart ultrasound). The classic route is **subxiphoid**: just below the xiphoid process, the needle aims upward toward the left shoulder.
levels.college:
**Pericardial anatomy.** The fibrous pericardium blends with the central tendon of the diaphragm below and with the adventitia of the great vessels above. It is anchored to the sternum by sternopericardial ligaments. The serous pericardium forms the parietal and visceral layers (the visceral layer is the **epicardium**). Its reflections create the **transverse sinus** (behind the aorta and pulmonary trunk) and the **oblique sinus** (behind the left atrium). The fibrous layer is supplied by the **phrenic nerves** (C3 to C5), so pericardial pain can be referred to the shoulder.

**Pathophysiology of tamponade.** The pericardial pressure-volume curve is flat at first and then rises steeply. Once fluid reaches the steep part, small additions cause large pressure rises.
- Intrapericardial pressure rises until it equals the diastolic filling pressures of the chambers.
- Right atrial collapse, then right ventricular diastolic collapse, appear on echo.
- **Pulsus paradoxus** is an exaggerated fall in systolic pressure on inspiration (more than 10 mmHg). Inspiration increases right-heart filling. Because total heart volume is fixed, the septum shifts left and left ventricular output drops (**ventricular interdependence**).
- The inferior vena cava is dilated and does not collapse with breathing.

**Approaches to pericardiocentesis:**
- **Subxiphoid**: the needle enters between the xiphoid and the left costal margin at about 30 to 45 degrees to the skin, aiming toward the left shoulder. It passes through the skin, linea alba or rectus sheath, and diaphragmatic attachments, staying extrapleural. Risks include the liver, the right ventricle and the abdomen.
- **Apical**: entering near the cardiac apex, which lies close to the left lung.
- **Parasternal**: the left 5th intercostal space, close to the sternal edge. The needle passes over the upper border of the rib to avoid the intercostal bundle, and must stay medial to the **internal thoracic artery**, which runs about 1 to 2 cm lateral to the sternal border.

Echo guidance picks the site where the fluid is deepest and closest to the skin, with no organ in the way.
levels.phd:
**Mechanics.** The fibrous pericardium is made of layered collagen with elastin, giving a J-shaped stress-strain curve. Chronic effusions cause stretching and remodelling of the sac, which moves the steep part of the curve to the right. This is why the speed at which fluid builds up predicts tamponade better than the volume does. Effective filling depends on **transmural pressure** (chamber pressure minus pericardial pressure), not on absolute intracavitary pressure. In tamponade, right atrial, right ventricular diastolic, pulmonary capillary wedge and pericardial pressures **equalize**, often at about 15 to 20 mmHg. The systemic venous waveform loses its **y descent**, because early diastolic filling is blocked. The x descent is preserved. By contrast, constrictive pericarditis shows a steep y descent (the square-root sign).

**Respiratory physiology.** Pulsus paradoxus arises from fixed total cardiac volume. Inspiratory falls in intrathoracic pressure are passed to the right heart but less to the pulmonary veins. Left ventricular filling therefore drops while right ventricular filling rises. On echo, this appears as exaggerated respiratory variation in transmitral and transtricuspid E waves. Mitral inflow variation of roughly 25% or more and tricuspid variation of roughly 40% or more are commonly cited. Pulsus paradoxus may be absent with an atrial septal defect, severe aortic regurgitation, positive-pressure ventilation, marked left ventricular hypertrophy or raised diastolic pressure, or a localized effusion.

**Regional tamponade.** After cardiac surgery, a clot may compress a single chamber, often the left or right atrium. Classic signs may then be absent, and transoesophageal echo is often needed to find it.

**Evolution of technique.** Blind subxiphoid puncture had substantial complication rates in older series. The Mayo Clinic echo-guided experience (Tsang and colleagues, more than 1,000 procedures) reported a total complication rate of about 4.7% with major complications of about 1.2%. It showed that the most frequent optimal entry site is apical or parasternal, not subxiphoid. Agitated saline injected through the needle confirms that its tip lies within the pericardial space. An indwelling pigtail catheter reduces the need for repeat drainage.

Anatomical hazards along the path include the right ventricle and the left anterior descending artery and its branches, the internal thoracic vessels, the liver and stomach, and the pleura (risking pneumothorax).
levels.expert:
**Diagnosis is clinical-echo integration.** Echo shows effusion size and chamber collapse. Tamponade, however, is a hemodynamic diagnosis. The 2015 ESC pericardial guidelines, and an earlier ESC triage score, weigh etiology, clinical status and imaging to judge urgency. For an unstable patient there is no need for a score. Pitfalls:
- **Low-pressure tamponade** occurs in hypovolemic patients (for example, those with dehydration or on dialysis). Jugular venous pressure looks normal, and filling pressures equalize at low values. Fluid can temporize, but drainage is still needed.
- An epicardial fat pad can mimic an anterior effusion.
- A **left pleural effusion** can be mistaken for pericardial fluid. The descending aorta helps tell them apart: pericardial fluid tracks anterior to it, while pleural fluid lies posterior.

**Hemodynamic management before drainage.** Positive-pressure ventilation and induction agents can trigger collapse by cutting venous return. Whenever possible, drain the effusion under local anaesthesia with the patient spontaneously breathing.

**Etiology dictates the route.** In traumatic hemopericardium and **type A aortic dissection**, needle drainage is generally inappropriate. In trauma, the definitive treatment is surgical: sternotomy, or emergency thoracotomy in arrest. Pericardiocentesis is only a bridge. In dissection, relieving tamponade can raise pressure and extend the tear, so emergency surgery is preferred. Free-wall rupture after myocardial infarction also needs surgery. Purulent pericarditis needs drainage, often surgically, plus antibiotics.

**Complications and nuances.**
- **Pericardial decompression syndrome** is rare and can follow drainage of large chronic effusions. It causes paradoxical ventricular dysfunction or pulmonary oedema. Staged drainage of large chronic effusions is often advised.
- Recurrent malignant effusions may need a **pericardial window**, either subxiphoid or video-assisted thoracoscopic.
- Effusions after procedures such as ablation, pacing-lead perforation and TAVI make up a growing share of drainage cases. Cath-lab teams often perform fluoroscopy plus echo guided drainage.

**Open questions.** It is still unclear whether routine extended catheter drainage reduces recurrence in all etiologies. Other open questions are whether intrapericardial therapies help in malignant effusion, and whether point-of-care ultrasound by non-cardiologists improves outcomes in emergencies.

keyPoints: The fibrous pericardium is stiff, so rapid fluid buildup compresses the heart
Rate of accumulation matters more than total volume
Beck's triad: hypotension, raised JVP, muffled heart sounds
Pulsus paradoxus reflects ventricular interdependence
Echo-guided pericardiocentesis: subxiphoid, apical or parasternal routes
Trauma and aortic dissection tamponade need surgery, not just a needle

kidTest.explain: Extra fluid in the bag presses on the heart.

advancedTest.q: A dialysis patient has tamponade on echo but normal JVP. The best explanation is:
choices: Constrictive pericarditis masking raised venous pressure
Regional clot compressing the left atrium
Fat pad mimicking an anterior effusion
advancedTest.explain: Hypovolemia lets pressures equalize at low values, so JVP looks normal.

advancedTest.q: Why is needle drainage generally avoided in tamponade from type A dissection?
choices: Blood in the sac clots too fast to aspirate
The effusion is usually too small to reach
The subxiphoid path crosses the aortic root

choices: Fluid tracking anterior to the descending aorta
Fluid that moves with each heartbeat

lessons.title: Inguinal and Femoral Hernias: Anatomical Distinctions

levels.kid:
Your tummy has a strong wall made of muscle layers, like a stack of blankets. Down low, near where your leg joins your body, there are a few small tunnels. They let tubes and blood vessels pass through to the legs and, in boys, to the testicles.

Sometimes a bit of the soft insides pushes into one of these tunnels and makes a bump. That bump is called a **hernia**.

There are two main kinds near the groin. An **inguinal hernia** pushes through a tunnel just above the crease of the leg. It is the most common kind, especially in boys and men. A **femoral hernia** squeezes through a smaller gap just below that crease. It is rarer, but it is more likely to get stuck.

Surgeons know exactly where each tunnel is, so they can fix the weak spot.
levels.hs:
A **hernia** is when tissue, often fat or a loop of intestine, pushes through a weak spot or opening in the wall that normally holds it in. The groin has two important openings.

The **inguinal canal** is a short diagonal tunnel, about 4 cm long, running through the lower abdominal wall just above the **inguinal ligament**. The inguinal ligament is a tough band stretching from the bony point at the front of the hip (the anterior superior iliac spine) to the pubic tubercle. In males the canal carries the **spermatic cord** down to the testis. In females it carries the round ligament of the uterus.

The **femoral canal** lies just *below* the inguinal ligament, on the inner side of the big femoral vein, as blood vessels pass into the thigh.

Two kinds of inguinal hernia:
- **Indirect**: enters the canal through its inner opening (the deep ring) and follows the cord, sometimes reaching the scrotum. This is the most common hernia in both sexes.
- **Direct**: pushes straight forward through a weak patch in the back wall of the canal.

A **femoral hernia** comes out through the femoral canal. It is more common in women, though inguinal hernias are still more common in women overall. Because the femoral ring is narrow and stiff, the bowel can get trapped and lose its blood supply. This is called **strangulation**, and it is a surgical emergency.
levels.college:
**Inguinal canal boundaries** (mnemonic MALT: two structures for each wall, top to bottom):
- **Superior wall (roof)**: Muscles: internal oblique and transversus abdominis arching fibers.
- **Anterior wall**: Aponeurosis of external oblique, reinforced laterally by internal oblique.
- **Inferior wall (floor)**: Ligaments: inguinal ligament and lacunar ligament.
- **Posterior wall**: Transversalis fascia, reinforced medially by the **conjoint tendon**.

The **deep ring** is an opening in the transversalis fascia, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels and just above the midpoint of the inguinal ligament. The **superficial ring** is a split in the external oblique aponeurosis, superolateral to the pubic tubercle.

**Hesselbach's (inguinal) triangle** has three borders: the inferior epigastric vessels laterally, the lateral edge of rectus abdominis medially, and the inguinal ligament inferiorly.
- **Indirect hernias** arise *lateral* to the inferior epigastric vessels. They pass through the deep ring inside the spermatic cord's coverings and often reflect a patent **processus vaginalis**. They are congenital in origin and are the usual type in infants.
- **Direct hernias** arise *medial* to the vessels, through Hesselbach's triangle. They are acquired from weakness of the transversalis fascia, usually in older men. They rarely enter the scrotum.

**Femoral canal**: it is the medial compartment of the femoral sheath. The lateral-to-medial order is NAVEL: nerve (outside the sheath), artery, vein, empty space, lymphatics. The canal contains fat and a lymph node (Cloquet's). The **femoral ring** has these borders:
- inguinal ligament anteriorly
- pectineal (Cooper's) ligament posteriorly
- lacunar ligament medially
- femoral vein laterally

Femoral hernias emerge *below and lateral* to the pubic tubercle, whereas inguinal hernias emerge above and medial to it. This is a key bedside distinction. The rigid ring explains why femoral hernias have high rates of incarceration and strangulation.
levels.phd:
Developmentally, the inguinal canal is the track of gonadal descent. The **gubernaculum** guides the testis through the abdominal wall, and an evagination of peritoneum, the **processus vaginalis**, precedes it. Each wall layer contributes a covering to the spermatic cord:
- transversalis fascia becomes the internal spermatic fascia
- internal oblique becomes the cremaster muscle and fascia
- external oblique aponeurosis becomes the external spermatic fascia

An indirect hernia sac acquires all three coverings. A direct sac acquires them incompletely or not at all. Failure of the processus to obliterate underlies pediatric indirect hernias and communicating hydroceles. It is commoner on the right, which has been linked to the later descent of the right testis.

The **myopectineal orifice of Fruchaud** unifies the anatomy. It is a single region bounded by:
- the arching muscles above
- the rectus medially
- iliopsoas laterally
- Cooper's ligament and the pecten pubis below

The inguinal ligament divides this orifice into inguinal and femoral parts, and only transversalis fascia closes it. All groin hernias are therefore failures of the same fascial barrier. This concept underpins the preperitoneal mesh repair.

Normal canal function depends on mechanisms. The **obliquity** of the canal lets intra-abdominal pressure press the posterior wall against the anterior wall. A **shutter mechanism** of the arching internal oblique and transversus lowers the roof onto the floor during contraction.

Acquired direct hernias have been associated with abnormalities of collagen. These include a lower ratio of type I to type III collagen in the transversalis fascia, along with smoking and connective tissue disorders. This is evidence that biology, not just mechanics, is involved.

On epidemiology, lifetime risk of groin hernia is roughly 27% in men and 3% in women. Femoral hernias are about 3-5% of groin hernias but cause a disproportionate share of emergency surgery. In some series a substantial fraction of femoral hernias present first as emergencies.

The **corona mortis** is a vascular anastomosis between the obturator and inferior epigastric or external iliac vessels. It crosses the superior pubic ramus near the lacunar ligament. Dividing the lacunar ligament to free a strangulated femoral hernia can tear an aberrant obturator artery, causing troublesome bleeding.
levels.expert:
**Diagnostic pitfalls**: Bedside methods such as the deep ring occlusion test and the side of finger impulse do a poor job of distinguishing direct from indirect hernias. Their accuracy is near chance in some studies, so management rarely depends on them. The clinically decisive distinction is **femoral vs inguinal**. In women, especially older women, a groin lump below the inguinal ligament with obstructive symptoms should be treated as femoral until proven otherwise. A **Richter hernia** traps only part of the bowel wall's circumference. It can strangulate without complete obstruction, delaying recognition. Ultrasound is first-line when the diagnosis is unclear. Dynamic MRI helps with occult hernias and athletic groin pain.

**Operative anatomy, open approach**: In Lichtenstein repair, mesh is fixed to the inguinal ligament shelving edge and the rectus sheath, with the cord passing through a slit. Three nerves lie in the field:
- **ilioinguinal nerve**, on the cord
- **iliohypogastric nerve**, deep to the external oblique
- **genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve**, with the cremasteric vessels

Identifying these nerves reduces chronic postherniorrhaphy pain. This pain affects roughly 10% of patients and is a leading reason for litigation. **McVay repair**, which uses Cooper's ligament, closes both the inguinal floor and the femoral ring.

**Laparoscopic approach (TEP/TAPP)**: The posterior view reorients everything. Key danger zones are:
- **Triangle of doom**: bounded by the vas deferens medially and the gonadal vessels laterally, containing the external iliac vessels. No tacks should be placed here.
- **Triangle of pain**: lateral to the gonadal vessels and below the iliopubic tract, containing the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve, the femoral branch of genitofemoral nerve and the femoral nerve. Placing tacks here causes neuralgia.

The mesh should cover the whole myopectineal orifice, which can reveal clinically unsuspected contralateral or femoral defects.

**Current guidance and open questions**: The HerniaSurg international guidelines (2018) endorse mesh repair for most adult hernias. They support watchful waiting for minimally symptomatic inguinal hernias in men, although many patients eventually cross over to surgery. Femoral hernias, given their strangulation risk, are repaired promptly. Female groin hernias are often managed laparoscopically so that occult femoral defects can be seen. Unresolved issues include:
- the best way to fix the mesh (glue vs tacks)
- whether lightweight mesh truly reduces pain
- whether robotic repair adds benefit beyond cost
- the best way to manage asymptomatic contralateral defects

keyPoints: Inguinal hernias exit above the inguinal ligament; femoral hernias exit below it
Indirect inguinal hernias pass through the deep ring, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels
Direct inguinal hernias push through Hesselbach's triangle, medial to those vessels
Femoral canal is the medial femoral sheath compartment (NAVEL), medial to the femoral vein
Femoral hernias are more common in women and strangulate often due to a rigid ring
Laparoscopic repair avoids the triangle of doom and triangle of pain

test.q: An indirect inguinal hernia enters the canal through the:
test.explain: Indirect hernias enter at the deep ring, an opening in the transversalis fascia, and follow the spermatic cord. The superficial ring is the exit point, not the entry.

test.q: Which structure forms the lateral border of Hesselbach's triangle?
test.explain: The inferior epigastric vessels form the lateral border. Rectus abdominis forms the medial border, and the inguinal ligament forms the inferior border.

test.q: A hernia arising medial to the inferior epigastric vessels in an older man is most likely:
test.explain: Direct hernias push through Hesselbach's triangle, which lies medial to the vessels. They are acquired weaknesses typical of older men.

test.q: The posterior wall of the inguinal canal is formed mainly by:
test.explain: Transversalis fascia, reinforced medially by the conjoint tendon, forms the posterior wall. The external oblique aponeurosis forms the anterior wall.

test.q: Which structure lies immediately lateral to the femoral canal?
test.explain: In the order NAVEL, the empty space (the canal) lies just medial to the femoral vein. The lacunar ligament forms the medial border.

test.q: Relative to the pubic tubercle, a femoral hernia typically appears:
test.explain: Femoral hernias emerge below the inguinal ligament, inferolateral to the pubic tubercle. Inguinal hernias lie above and medial to it.

test.q: Why do femoral hernias strangulate more often than inguinal ones?
choices: Their sac lacks a peritoneal lining
The femoral ring is narrow and rigid
test.explain: The femoral ring is narrow and bounded by unyielding ligaments, which trap herniated bowel. The sac is lined by peritoneum, like other hernias.

test.q: Persistence of which structure underlies most pediatric indirect hernias?
test.explain: A patent processus vaginalis leaves a peritoneal pathway through the deep ring. The urachus and vitelline duct relate to the bladder and gut instead.

test.q: In females, the inguinal canal transmits the:
test.explain: The round ligament of the uterus passes through the canal to the labium majus. It is the female counterpart of the gubernacular path.

test.q: What is the general term for a hernia whose trapped bowel loses its blood supply?
test.explain: Strangulation means the blood supply is cut off. It is a surgical emergency.

test.q: The femoral ring is bounded posteriorly by the pectineal, or ___'s, ligament.
test.explain: The pectineal (Cooper's) ligament runs along the pecten pubis and forms the floor of the femoral ring.

test.q: The medial reinforcement of the inguinal canal's posterior wall is the ___ tendon.
test.explain: The conjoint tendon is formed by the fused aponeuroses of the internal oblique and transversus abdominis.

kidTest.q: What is a hernia?
choices: A cut on the skin of the lower belly
Insides pushing through a weak spot
A broken bone deep inside the hip area
kidTest.explain: A hernia happens when soft tissue pushes through a weak place in the body wall.

kidTest.q: Which kind of groin hernia is the most common?
kidTest.explain: Inguinal hernias are the most common, especially in boys and men.

kidTest.q: Where does a femoral hernia come out?
kidTest.explain: A femoral hernia squeezes through a small gap below the crease.

kidTest.q: Why are femoral hernias worrying?
choices: They are more likely to get stuck
They make the leg bone weak
kidTest.explain: Their gap is small, so tissue can get stuck there.

kidTest.q: The groin openings are like small t _ _ _ _ _ s that let tubes and vessels pass through.
kidTest.explain: The lesson describes these openings as tunnels through the tummy wall.

advancedTest.q: At laparoscopy, a defect lies lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels above the iliopubic tract. The sac most likely:
choices: Enters the femoral ring medial to the femoral vein
Herniates through the obturator foramen beneath the pubis
Passes through Hesselbach's triangle without cord coverings
Follows the cord within internal spermatic fascia
advancedTest.explain: A defect lateral to the vessels is at the deep ring, which makes it indirect. An indirect sac acquires internal spermatic fascia from transversalis fascia and runs with the cord.

advancedTest.q: Why does the myopectineal orifice concept favor preperitoneal mesh covering the whole region?
choices: Direct hernias develop from a patent processus vaginalis in adults
Transversalis fascia alone closes both inguinal and femoral parts
The inguinal ligament forms the posterior wall of each hernia site
Femoral hernias arise from failure of the external oblique aponeurosis
advancedTest.explain: All groin hernias are failures of the same transversalis fascia barrier. Mesh covering the whole orifice therefore addresses the direct, indirect and femoral sites at once.

advancedTest.q: While dividing the lacunar ligament to free a strangulated femoral hernia, brisk bleeding occurs. The likely source is:
choices: The superficial epigastric vein in fat of the canal
The deep circumflex iliac artery near the ring
The femoral vein lying medially in the canal
An aberrant obturator artery of the corona mortis
advancedTest.explain: The corona mortis can run across the superior pubic ramus near the lacunar ligament. The femoral vein lies lateral to the canal, not medial.

advancedTest.q: A patient has burning lateral thigh pain after laparoscopic repair. The most likely cause is:
choices: Tacks placed medial to the vas in the triangle of doom
Mesh fixed to the rectus sheath above the pubic tubercle
Tacks below the iliopubic tract lateral to gonadal vessels
Injury to the ilioinguinal nerve lying on the spermatic cord
advancedTest.explain: The triangle of pain contains the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve. The ilioinguinal nerve is the usual worry in open repair, and the triangle of doom risks injury to vessels rather than nerves.

lessons.title: Abdominal Incisions, Paracentesis Sites and Laparoscopic Ports

levels.kid:
Imagine the belly wall is like a layered sandwich: skin, a cushion of fat, strong muscle sheets, and a thin inner lining. Inside are the stomach, liver and long loops of gut.

When surgeons need to get inside, they choose where to cut very carefully. The middle line of the belly is a great spot because it has a tough strip with few blood vessels, a bit like the seam on a jacket.

Sometimes fluid builds up in the belly. Doctors can drain it with a thin needle placed low on the left side, where it stays clear of big blood vessels and the liver.

In keyhole surgery, doctors make tiny holes, fill the belly with gas like a balloon, and look inside with a camera.
levels.hs:
Surgeons and doctors enter the abdomen in three main ways: open incisions, needle drainage, and keyhole (laparoscopic) surgery. Each relies on knowing the layers of the **anterior abdominal wall**: skin, fat, the muscles (rectus abdominis in front; external oblique, internal oblique and transversus abdominis at the sides), transversalis fascia, and the **peritoneum** lining the cavity.

- **Midline laparotomy**: a cut through the **linea alba**, the fibrous seam where the muscle sheaths meet. It is quick, nearly bloodless and gives access to the whole abdomen.
- **Transverse and oblique incisions** follow the skin's natural tension lines and the direction of nerves, so they heal neatly. The low transverse **Pfannenstiel** incision is used for caesarean sections.

**Paracentesis** means draining fluid (called **ascites**) from the peritoneal cavity, often in people with liver cirrhosis. The usual site is the **left lower quadrant**, lateral to the rectus muscle. This avoids the **inferior epigastric artery**, which runs up behind the rectus, and stays away from the liver and a full bladder.

**Laparoscopy** uses small **ports** (tubes called trocars). The first is usually placed at the **umbilicus**, where the wall is thinnest. Carbon dioxide gas inflates the abdomen (pneumoperitoneum) so the camera and instruments have room.

Example: removing a gallbladder is now usually done through four small ports instead of a large cut under the ribs.
levels.college:
Choice of abdominal access balances exposure, speed, and preservation of the wall's vessels and nerves.

**Wall anatomy that matters**
- Segmental nerves T7-T12 and L1 (thoracoabdominal, subcostal, iliohypogastric, ilioinguinal) run between internal oblique and transversus abdominis (the **transversus abdominis plane**) and enter the rectus sheath laterally. Vertical incisions lateral to the rectus can denervate and weaken the muscle.
- The **superior and inferior epigastric arteries** anastomose within the rectus sheath, posterior to the muscle. The inferior epigastric arises from the external iliac and runs roughly from the mid-inguinal point toward the umbilicus.
- Below the **arcuate line** (about a third of the way from umbilicus to pubis), all aponeuroses pass anterior to rectus, leaving only transversalis fascia behind.

**Incisions**
- **Midline**: through linea alba; fast, extensile, good for trauma. It carries a higher incisional hernia risk.
- **Paramedian**: incises the anterior rectus sheath and retracts rectus laterally, preserving its nerves; now uncommon.
- **Kocher (right subcostal)**: for liver and biliary access; parallel to the costal margin.
- **Gridiron/Lanz** at **McBurney's point**: muscle-splitting appendicectomy that follows fibre directions.
- **Pfannenstiel**: transverse skin and anterior sheath, then the recti are separated vertically in the midline.

**Paracentesis**
The preferred site is about two finger-breadths medial and superior to the anterior superior iliac spine, lateral to rectus. This site avoids the inferior epigastric vessels, and the ascites is often deeper and the wall thinner there than in the midline. A **Z-track** technique offsets skin and peritoneal punctures to limit leakage. Ultrasound guidance can identify fluid pockets, bowel and wall vessels.

**Laparoscopic ports**
The primary port is typically umbilical, by open (**Hasson**) or Veress needle entry. **Palmer's point** (left upper quadrant, about 3 cm below the costal margin in the midclavicular line) is an alternative when adhesions are suspected. Accessory ports are placed under direct vision, lateral to the rectus or in the midline, avoiding the inferior epigastric vessels, which can often be seen through the peritoneum. Port positions are arranged so instruments triangulate on the target.
levels.phd:
Incision design rests on three anatomical principles: follow the **Langer/Kraissl tension lines** for cosmesis, preserve the segmental neurovascular bundles for function, and close aponeurosis rather than muscle for strength.

**Linea alba biomechanics.** The linea alba is a decussating meshwork of collagen fibres from the three flat-muscle aponeuroses. Its relative avascularity eases entry but slows healing. Incisional hernia follows a substantial minority of midline laparotomies. The STITCH trial (Deerenberg et al., Lancet 2015) showed that a **small-bites** closure, roughly 5 mm bites placed about 5 mm apart with a suture-to-wound length ratio of at least 4:1 (Jenkins' rule), reduces hernia compared with large bites. The PRIMA trial supported prophylactic onlay mesh in high-risk patients.

**Vascular corridors.** The inferior epigastric artery enters the sheath at the arcuate line and ascends; the superficial epigastric artery runs in subcutaneous fat. Imaging studies of the wall place the deep epigastric vessels mostly about 4-8 cm from the midline. That separation underlies the safety of lateral paracentesis and lateral port placement. In portal hypertension, recanalized paraumbilical veins and abdominal-wall varices (**caput medusae**) add risk to midline puncture.

**Paracentesis physiology.** Ascites pools in dependent regions. The left lower quadrant is favoured over the right because of caecal gas and appendicectomy scars on the right. Coagulopathy measured by INR does not reliably predict bleeding in cirrhosis, and routine plasma correction is not recommended. Serious haemorrhage is rare but usually arises from injury to an inferior epigastric artery or a varix.

**Laparoscopic entry.** Around half of laparoscopic major-vessel and bowel injuries occur at primary entry. At the umbilicus, the aortic bifurcation lies near L4, roughly beneath the umbilicus. In thin patients the aorta may be only a few centimetres deep, so the Veress needle is angled caudally. Cochrane reviews have not shown a clear safety advantage of open over closed entry for major vascular injury, although open entry eliminates failed insufflation. Port-site hernias mainly occur at fascial defects 10 mm or larger, especially at the umbilicus, so those defects are usually closed.
levels.expert:
Practical decision-making increasingly depends on imaging, patient-specific anatomy and frailty-aware closure.

**Incision selection in context.** In damage-control trauma, the midline remains standard because it is extensile from xiphoid to pubis. Prior incisions dictate future entry. Re-entering through an old midline scar risks enterotomy where bowel is adherent to the undersurface. Many surgeons start just beyond the scar's end to enter virgin peritoneum. Transverse incisions in children, whose abdomen is wider than it is long, give excellent exposure. For flap surgeons, preserving the deep inferior epigastric perforators matters: a prior paramedian or lateral port may compromise a future **DIEP** breast-reconstruction flap.

**Paracentesis pitfalls.**
- Ultrasound with colour Doppler can map the inferior epigastric course. Its route varies, and it may lie further lateral in obese patients and in those with tense ascites.
- Avoid surgical scars (adherent bowel), cellulitis, distended bladder and visible collaterals.
- Delayed rectus sheath haematoma can present hours later with falling haemoglobin and a palpable mass, sometimes with haemodynamic instability. CT angiography and embolization are first-line rescue.
- In large-volume drainage, albumin replacement is used to reduce post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction. That is a physiology decision, not an anatomical one.

**Port strategy.** The **baseball-diamond** principle places the camera behind the working ports, which converge on the target at angles of about 60 degrees. In obese patients the umbilicus migrates caudally relative to the bifurcation, so ports are referenced to bony landmarks. Optical-access trocars allow layer-by-layer visualization. In pregnancy, entry is shifted cephalad by fundal height or moved to Palmer's point. Robotic platforms need wider port spacing, often about 8 cm, to avoid arm collision.

**Open questions.**
- Should prophylactic mesh be routine after midline laparotomy?
- Do small-bites closures hold up in emergency surgery?
- Do single-incision and natural-orifice approaches (NOTES) truly reduce wall morbidity, or do they trade it for a higher umbilical hernia rate? Meta-analyses suggest more hernias after single-incision surgery.

For a future neurosurgeon, abdominal access appears directly in ventriculoperitoneal shunt placement. Laparoscopic-assisted peritoneal catheter insertion confirms intraperitoneal position and may reduce distal malposition.

keyPoints: Midline laparotomy through the avascular linea alba is fast and extensile but prone to incisional hernia
Transverse/oblique incisions follow tension lines and spare segmental nerves T7-L1
Paracentesis: left lower quadrant, lateral to rectus, avoiding the inferior epigastric artery
Inferior epigastric vessels run behind rectus within its sheath from the external iliac
Laparoscopic primary port is usually umbilical; Palmer's point is an alternative
Small-bites closure (STITCH) and closing 10 mm or larger port fascia reduce hernias

test.q: A midline laparotomy divides which structure?
test.explain: The midline incision passes through the linea alba, the fibrous seam where the aponeuroses meet. The semilunar line marks the lateral border of rectus.

test.q: Why is the left lower quadrant preferred for paracentesis?
choices: The liver lies deep to it
test.explain: A site lateral to rectus avoids the inferior epigastric artery. It also stays clear of the liver and bladder.

test.q: The inferior epigastric artery arises from the:
test.explain: The inferior epigastric artery branches from the external iliac and ascends behind rectus. The superior epigastric continues from the internal thoracic artery.

test.q: The Pfannenstiel incision is classically used for:
test.explain: The low transverse Pfannenstiel incision is standard for caesarean sections. Appendicectomy uses a gridiron or Lanz incision.

test.q: A Kocher incision runs parallel to the:
test.explain: The Kocher incision is a right subcostal incision used for liver and biliary access.

test.q: Where is the usual primary laparoscopic port placed?
test.explain: The umbilicus is the thinnest part of the abdominal wall and is centrally placed for viewing.

test.q: Below the arcuate line, the posterior rectus sheath consists of:
test.explain: Below the arcuate line, all the aponeuroses pass in front of rectus. Only transversalis fascia remains behind it.

test.q: Vertical incisions lateral to rectus risk weakness mainly by:
test.explain: The segmental nerves T7-L1 enter rectus laterally. Cutting them denervates the muscle and weakens it.

test.q: Palmer's point is used for laparoscopic entry when:
test.explain: This left upper quadrant site avoids periumbilical adhesions, such as those from previous surgery.

test.q: The gas used to inflate the abdomen in laparoscopy is carbon ___.
test.explain: CO2 creates the pneumoperitoneum. It is non-flammable and rapidly absorbed.

test.q: What is the term for abnormal fluid in the peritoneal cavity?
test.explain: Ascites is commonly due to cirrhosis and is drained by paracentesis.

test.q: An appendicectomy incision is centred on ___'s point.
test.explain: McBurney's point guides the muscle-splitting gridiron or Lanz incision.

kidTest.q: Why is the middle line of the belly a good place to cut?
choices: It is closest to the heart
kidTest.explain: The middle seam is tough and has few blood vessels, a bit like the seam on a jacket.

kidTest.q: Where do doctors often put the needle to drain belly fluid?
kidTest.explain: Low on the left side keeps the needle clear of big blood vessels and the liver.

kidTest.q: What do doctors put in the belly during keyhole surgery?
kidTest.explain: Gas puffs up the belly like a balloon so the camera can see.

kidTest.q: What helps doctors see inside during keyhole surgery?
kidTest.explain: A small camera goes in through one of the tiny holes.

kidTest.q: The thin inner lining of the belly is the p _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: The peritoneum is the inner lining of the belly.

advancedTest.q: Why does lateral paracentesis carry less bleeding risk than a puncture at the lateral rectus border?
choices: The lateral wall receives a much poorer blood supply
Ascites collects mostly in the midline of the abdomen
Deep epigastric vessels lie 4-8 cm from the midline
Coagulopathy is corrected by lateral body positioning
advancedTest.explain: The deep epigastric vessels run near the edge of rectus, so a puncture lateral to the muscle clears them. Ascites pools in dependent regions, not mainly in the midline.

advancedTest.q: The STITCH trial's reduction in incisional hernia is best explained by:
choices: Wider bites that grip more of the underlying muscle
Small, close bites in aponeurosis with more suture
Closing the peritoneum as its own separate layer
Routine prophylactic mesh placed in each laparotomy
advancedTest.explain: Small bites placed close together in aponeurosis, with a suture-to-wound ratio of at least 4:1, distribute tension better. Mesh was the subject of the separate PRIMA trial.

advancedTest.q: In a thin patient, why is the Veress needle angled caudally at the umbilicus?
choices: The aortic bifurcation may lie shallow beneath it
The liver edge is reached more directly that way
The linea alba is thin or absent at that level
The bladder can be decompressed through that path
advancedTest.explain: The aortic bifurcation lies near L4, roughly beneath the umbilicus, and may be only a few centimetres deep. Angling the needle away from it reduces the risk of vascular injury.

advancedTest.q: A paramedian or lateral port in a patient planning breast reconstruction matters because it may:
choices: Divide the linea alba in the lower abdomen
Injure the internal thoracic artery branches
Trigger caput medusae around the umbilicus
advancedTest.explain: A DIEP flap relies on the deep inferior epigastric perforators. Earlier incisions or ports through rectus can damage them.

lessons.title: Trunk Fascial Plane Blocks and Thoracolumbar Epidural Anatomy

levels.kid:
Your chest and tummy have lots of tiny nerves. They run between your ribs like wires tucked between layers of a sandwich. These nerves carry "ouch" messages to your spinal cord.

After an operation, doctors want to stop those ouch messages. One way is to put numbing medicine between two muscle layers, right where the nerve wires travel. The medicine spreads along the layer like jam spreading in a sandwich. This is called a **nerve block**.

Another way is to put medicine just outside the bag of fluid that holds the spinal cord. That space is called the **epidural** space.

Doctors use an ultrasound camera to see the layers. That way the needle goes to the right spot safely.
levels.hs:
The skin, muscles and ribs of the trunk get their feeling from **spinal nerves** T1 to L1. Each one leaves the spine and splits into a **dorsal ramus** (to the back) and a **ventral ramus**. The ventral rami become the **intercostal nerves**, which run in a groove under each rib, between muscle layers. The lower ones (T7 to T11) continue forward into the abdominal wall.

A **fascial plane block** uses this layout. Fascia is a sheet of connective tissue covering muscles. Instead of aiming at one nerve, the doctor injects **local anesthetic** (numbing medicine) into the plane between two muscles where the nerves travel. The drug spreads and numbs several nerves at once. Ultrasound shows the muscle layers and the needle tip.

A real example is the **transversus abdominis plane (TAP) block**. Anesthetic goes between the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles. It numbs the front of the abdominal wall after surgeries such as a cesarean section.

The other major option is a **thoracic epidural**. A needle passes between vertebrae, through the **ligamentum flavum**, into the **epidural space**. This space lies just outside the dura, the tough covering of the spinal cord. A thin catheter is left in place to give continuous pain relief. Epidurals cover both the body wall and the internal organs. Most fascial plane blocks mainly numb the wall.
levels.college:
**Segmental innervation.** Thoracoabdominal wall sensation comes from T1 to L1 spinal nerves. Each nerve divides into a dorsal ramus (paraspinal muscles and skin) and a ventral ramus. Ventral rami run as intercostal nerves in the **costal groove**, between the innermost and internal intercostal muscles. The vein, artery and nerve lie in that order from above down (VAN). Each nerve gives a **lateral cutaneous branch** near the midaxillary line and ends as an **anterior cutaneous branch**. T7 to T11 (thoracoabdominal nerves) plus the subcostal nerve (T12) run between the internal oblique and transversus abdominis. Iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves come from L1. Visceral pain travels with sympathetic fibres through the paravertebral region, not along the wall.

**Key fascial plane blocks:**
- **Paravertebral block (PVB):** the wedge-shaped space bounded by parietal pleura in front, the superior costotransverse ligament behind, and vertebral body and disc medially. It reaches spinal nerves near their roots, sympathetic chain included. The main risk is pneumothorax.
- **Erector spinae plane (ESP) block:** injection deep to erector spinae, onto the transverse process.
- **Serratus anterior plane block:** superficial or deep to serratus at the midaxillary line, targeting lateral cutaneous branches. Used for rib fractures and breast surgery.
- **PECS I and II:** between pectoralis major and minor (lateral and medial pectoral nerves), then toward serratus.
- **TAP block:** between internal oblique and transversus abdominis, giving somatic analgesia only.
- **Rectus sheath block:** behind the rectus muscle, for midline incisions.
- **Quadratus lumborum (QL) blocks:** around quadratus lumborum. Some spread toward the thoracic paravertebral space.

**Thoracolumbar epidural.** Midline layers from skin inward: skin, subcutaneous tissue, supraspinous ligament, interspinous ligament, ligamentum flavum, epidural space, then dura. Thoracic spinous processes are steeply angled from about T5 to T8, so a **paramedian** approach is often easier. The **loss-of-resistance** technique tells the operator when the needle has entered the space. Epidurals give somatic and visceral analgesia, but they also cause sympathetic blockade and therefore hypotension.
levels.phd:
**The epidural space.** It is not a uniform tube. It is a discontinuous potential space holding fat, the internal vertebral (Batson's) venous plexus, lymphatics and segmental arteries. It is widest posteriorly in the lumbar region, about 5 to 6 mm at L2 to L3, and narrower at mid-thoracic levels. The **ligamentum flavum** is thickest in the lumbar region. In the midline, the left and right ligamenta flava may fail to fuse; gaps are reported in a substantial minority at thoracic levels. Unfused midline gaps can blunt the loss-of-resistance cue. The thoracic spinal cord lies close behind the dura, so a needle that goes too far risks direct cord injury. Lumbar epidurals placed below the conus have no such risk. The conus usually ends near L1 to L2.

Drug moves from the epidural space to the cord mainly by crossing the dura and arachnoid. The **arachnoid** is the main diffusion barrier. Lipid solubility sets the balance between segmental and rostral spread. Lipophilic opioids act more segmentally than hydrophilic morphine.

**How fascial plane blocks work.** The approach rests on hydrodissection: a volume-dependent spread through a compartment. It is not a precise perineural injection. That raises a mechanistic question for blocks placed far from nerve roots. The ESP block (Forero 2016) is the main example. Cadaver dye studies show reliable spread over the dorsal rami. Spread into the paravertebral and epidural spaces, through the costotransverse foramen and between intertransverse ligaments, is inconsistent. This mismatch helps explain why clinical results vary. Some authors suggest that systemic absorption of local anesthetic, or effects on fascial mechanoreceptors, contribute to the analgesia.

The QL block family shows the same uncertainty. Its anterior (transmuscular) approach can spread under the arcuate ligaments, past the diaphragm, into the thoracic paravertebral space. That may explain reported visceral analgesia, though results differ between studies. The TAP block, by contrast, gives somatic cover of roughly T10 to L1 with a lateral approach. A subcostal approach extends it toward T6 to T9. Duration is limited.

Terminology became chaotic as more blocks were described. An ASRA/ESRA Delphi consensus (El-Boghdadly et al., 2021) standardised names and target sonoanatomy for abdominal and chest wall blocks.
levels.expert:
**Choosing a technique.** Thoracic epidural analgesia was long the standard for open thoracotomy and laparotomy. Its use is falling. Minimally invasive surgery and enhanced-recovery pathways have shifted priorities. For video-assisted thoracic surgery (VATS), PROSPECT guidance favours paravertebral or ESP blocks over epidurals. Paravertebral block gives analgesia similar to an epidural after thoracotomy, with less hypotension, urinary retention and nausea. Real-world epidural failure rates are often quoted at about 20 to 30%. Causes include catheter migration, one-sided block and catheters that never entered the space.

**Pitfalls and safety:**
- **Anticoagulation:** epidural hematoma is rare but devastating. Insertion and catheter removal must follow ASRA timing rules for anticoagulants. Deep blocks such as paravertebral and lumbar plexus blocks are treated as neuraxial-like in risk. Superficial plane blocks are generally preferred when coagulation is uncertain.
- **Local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST):** large-volume plane blocks, especially bilateral and continuous catheters, can produce high plasma levels. Intercostal and serratus sites absorb fastest. Lipid emulsion should be immediately available.
- **Level error:** counting ribs or spinous processes by palpation is unreliable. Ultrasound pre-scanning improves accuracy.
- **Hypotension:** this follows from sympathetic block in epidural and bilateral paravertebral techniques. It is relevant for hypovolemic trauma patients.

**Recent developments.** Rib-fracture care is a growth area. Serratus and ESP catheters are attractive here because anticoagulated or coagulopathic trauma patients may not be suitable for an epidural. Mortality benefit is still unproven. Liposomal bupivacaine has had mixed trial results for prolonging plane blocks. Many trials compare a block with no block rather than with good multimodal analgesia. That design inflates the apparent effect. Sham-controlled trials are needed and are now increasing.

**Open questions.** Does the ESP block give clinically useful visceral analgesia? What explains the wide variation in individual spread, including fascial continuity, injection volume and pressure? Can a few validated blocks replace the many named variants?

**Neurosurgical relevance.** ESP blocks are now used in multilevel spine fusion, with reported reductions in opioid use. Thoracolumbar epidural anatomy is the same anatomy a neurosurgeon dissects in laminectomy: the ligamentum flavum, the epidural veins and the dural sac.

keyPoints: Trunk wall sensation comes from T1 to L1 spinal nerves, segment by segment
Intercostal nerves run in the costal groove below the vein and artery (VAN)
Fascial plane blocks spread local anesthetic in a plane between muscles to numb several nerves
TAP block lies between internal oblique and transversus abdominis and numbs the wall only
Epidural layers: skin, supraspinous, interspinous, ligamentum flavum, epidural space, dura
Epidurals and paravertebral blocks reach visceral pain fibres but can cause hypotension

test.q: A TAP block injects local anesthetic between which two muscles?
choices: Rectus abdominis and its posterior sheath
test.explain: The thoracoabdominal nerves travel in the plane between internal oblique and transversus abdominis, which is the TAP target.

test.q: In the costal groove, what is the order of structures from superior to inferior?
test.explain: VAN: the vein is highest, then the artery, and the nerve is lowest and most exposed.

test.q: During a midline epidural, which ligament is crossed just before entering the epidural space?
test.explain: The ligamentum flavum is the last ligament before the epidural space. The posterior longitudinal ligament lies anterior to the dural sac.

test.q: Why do most abdominal wall plane blocks, such as the TAP block, fail to relieve visceral pain?
choices: They are injected deep to the parietal peritoneum
They act on the dorsal rami of spinal nerves
They spread up into the cervical region
They miss the sympathetic paravertebral pathway
test.explain: Visceral afferents travel with sympathetic fibres through the paravertebral region, which wall-only blocks do not reach.

test.q: What is the main risk specific to a thoracic paravertebral block?
test.explain: The parietal pleura forms the anterior wall of the paravertebral space, so the needle can puncture it.

test.q: The erector spinae plane block places local anesthetic deep to erector spinae onto the:
test.explain: In the ESP block, the needle contacts the transverse process and the injectate spreads in the plane beneath the muscle.

test.q: Why is a paramedian approach often chosen for mid-thoracic epidurals?
choices: The epidural space is widest there
The ligamentum flavum is absent there
The spinal cord ends at that level
test.explain: Steeply sloping spinous processes at roughly T5 to T8 block a midline path, so going slightly to one side is easier.

test.q: A common side effect of thoracic epidurals that results from sympathetic blockade is:
test.explain: Blocking sympathetic outflow dilates blood vessels, so blood pressure falls.

test.q: A serratus anterior plane block mainly targets which nerve branches?
test.explain: The lateral cutaneous branches arise near the midaxillary line, which is where the serratus block is placed.

test.q: Blocks such as the TAP block work by spreading local anesthetic within a fascial ___ between muscles rather than at one nerve.
test.explain: The drug spreads through the plane by hydrodissection and reaches several nerves at once.

test.q: Which technique uses a sudden easing of syringe pressure to show the needle has entered the epidural space?
test.explain: Pressure on the syringe suddenly gives way when the needle tip leaves the ligamentum flavum and enters the epidural space.

test.q: Which spinal segments supply sensation to the thoracoabdominal wall (give the range)?
test.explain: Spinal nerves T1 through L1 supply the trunk wall segment by segment.

kidTest.q: What do the nerves in your chest and tummy carry?
kidTest.explain: Nerves carry pain messages to the spinal cord.

kidTest.q: Where do doctors put numbing medicine in a nerve block?
kidTest.explain: The medicine goes between layers, where the nerve wires travel.

kidTest.q: What does the medicine do once it is between the layers?
choices: It stays put in one small dot
It soaks straight into the muscle
kidTest.explain: It spreads like jam in a sandwich and reaches several nerves.

kidTest.q: What tool helps doctors see the layers?
kidTest.explain: Ultrasound shows the layers so the needle goes to the right place.

kidTest.q: The space just outside the spinal cord's bag is the e _ _ _ _ _ _ _ space.
kidTest.explain: Medicine placed in the epidural space can block pain messages.

advancedTest.q: Cadaver studies of the ESP block show reliable dorsal ramus staining but inconsistent paravertebral spread. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: Variable ventral or sympathetic coverage helps explain inconsistent clinical effect
Dorsal ramus coverage alone accounts for the analgesia after laparotomy
The ESP block gives dense visceral analgesia in most patients
Injection volume has no influence on where the drug spreads
advancedTest.explain: Visceral and ventral-ramus analgesia needs paravertebral or epidural spread. When that spread is variable, the clinical results are variable too.

advancedTest.q: A coagulopathic trauma patient has multiple unilateral rib fractures. Which approach best balances analgesia and bleeding risk?
advancedTest.explain: Superficial plane blocks are compressible and avoid the neuraxis, which matters when coagulation is uncertain. Epidural and paravertebral techniques carry hematoma risk.

advancedTest.q: Why might the anterior QL block give more visceral analgesia than a lateral TAP block?
choices: It spreads beneath the diaphragm to the paravertebral space
It is injected directly into the peritoneal cavity near the gut
It blocks the vagus nerve where it passes through the diaphragm
It anesthetises both rectus sheaths and the nerves inside them
advancedTest.explain: Spread under the arcuate ligaments, past the diaphragm, can reach the thoracic paravertebral space, where sympathetic fibres run. A TAP block stays in the wall.

advancedTest.q: Many trials of a new plane block compare it with no block rather than with optimised multimodal analgesia. What is the main consequence?
choices: The trials eliminate most of the placebo effect
The trials likely overstate the block's added benefit
The results reliably show a reduction in mortality
The trials underestimate how toxic local anesthetics are
advancedTest.explain: A weak comparator inflates the apparent effect size. Sham-controlled trials against good multimodal care give a truer estimate.
